hints: Focus on what the water actually receives, start by working out the heat needed to warm the water with q = mcΔT.
The water needs about 92 kJ, but the burner is only 47% efficient, so the total heat released by burning must be much larger.
Link that total heat to moles of butane using 2877 kJ per mole, then convert moles to grams with Mr = 58.
walkthrough:
**Find the heat the water must gain**

Think like the water first. It needs heat to go from 12 C to 100 C, so find the temperature rise and use q = mcΔT.

$$\Delta T = 100 - 12 = 88 \text{ } ^{\circ}\text{C}$$
$$q = mc\Delta T = 250 \times 4.18 \times 88 = 91960 \text{ J} = 92.0 \text{ kJ (approx)}$$

**Allow for the 47% efficiency**

Only 47% of the combustion heat reaches the water, so the burner must release more heat in total. Divide by 0.47.

$$q_{total} = \frac{q_{water}}{0.47} = \frac{92.0}{0.47} \approx 195.7 \text{ kJ}$$

**Convert heat released to mass of butane**

One mole of butane releases 2877 kJ on complete combustion. Find moles needed, then change to mass using mass = moles x Mr.

$$n(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}) = \frac{195.7}{2877} \approx 0.0680 \text{ mol}$$
$$m = n \times M_r = 0.0680 \times 58 \approx 3.94 \text{ g}$$

options.A: This is the number of moles of butane, about 0.068 mol, not the mass. You must multiply by Mr = 58 to get grams.
options.B: This is what you get if you forget the 47% efficiency. It uses only the 92 kJ gained by water, giving about 1.85 g, which is too small because over half the heat is lost.
options.C: Correct. Water needs about 92.0 kJ, so total combustion heat is 92.0 / 0.47 = 195.7 kJ. Moles = 195.7 / 2877 = 0.0680 mol, mass = 0.0680 x 58 = 3.94 g.
options.D: This comes from using 100 C as the temperature change instead of 88 C. The rise is 100 - 12 = 88 C, so using 100 overestimates the heat and gives about 4.48 g.
